title: Check your oil level
summary: A two-minute check that catches low oil before it damages the engine. Do it about once a month.
video_query: how to check engine oil level
tools: A quart of the right oil, only if you need to add some
intro:
Oil is what keeps the metal parts inside your engine from grinding against each other. Most cars slowly use a little oil between oil changes, and some leak or burn it faster as they get older. If the level gets too low, the engine can overheat and wear out quickly, which is one of the most expensive things that can go wrong with a car.

The good news is that checking it takes about two minutes and no special skills. Doing it once a month, and before any long road trip, is one of the best habits a car owner can have.
prep: All you really need is a paper towel or an old rag to wipe the dipstick clean. If it turns out you're low, you'll also want a quart of oil and a funnel. To find the right oil, look in your owner's manual (search for "engine oil" or "capacity"). It will list something like 0W-20 or 5W-30. That code describes how thick the oil is, and using the one your manual recommends matters, so buy that exact type. Any auto parts store or big-box store carries it, usually for less than $10 a quart.
safety: If you've just been driving, parts of the engine stay hot for a while. Keep your hands away from the metal pipes and the radiator, and give the car a few minutes to cool before reaching in.

steps.title: Park on flat ground and turn off the engine
steps.body: Oil sits in a pan at the bottom of the engine, and if the car is parked on a slope, the oil tilts to one side and the reading won't be accurate. Find a level spot, turn the car off, and if you just drove, wait about 5 to 10 minutes. That gives the oil time to drain back down into the pan so you get a true reading.

steps.title: Open the hood and find the dipstick
steps.body: Pull the hood release lever inside the car (usually near the driver's left knee), then find the second latch under the front edge of the hood and lift. The dipstick is a long, thin metal rod tucked into the engine with a loop or handle on top. The handle is almost always bright yellow or orange, and it often has a little oil-can symbol on it. If you can't find it, your owner's manual has a picture of the engine bay with it labeled.

steps.title: Pull it out and wipe it clean
steps.body: Pull the dipstick all the way out. The first time you pull it, the oil will be smeared up and down the stick from the engine moving, so this first look isn't accurate. Wipe the end of it completely clean with your paper towel.

steps.title: Put it back in, then pull it out again
steps.body: Slide the dipstick all the way back into its tube until the handle sits in place exactly like it was. Then pull it straight back out and hold it level so the oil doesn't run.

steps.title: Read the level
steps.body: Near the tip of the dipstick you'll see two small marks. They might be two holes, two lines, the letters L and H (low and high), or a crosshatched patch. The oil should leave a wet line somewhere between those two marks. Anywhere in that range is fine, and near the upper mark is ideal. If the oil only reaches the lower mark, or doesn't reach it at all, you need to add some.

steps.title: Look at the color
steps.body: While you have the dipstick out, look at the oil itself. Fresh oil is a see-through amber, like honey, and it gradually turns dark brown or black as it's used. That's normal. What isn't normal is oil that looks milky or light brown like coffee with cream, or that feels gritty when you rub a drop between your fingers. Either of those is a sign of a bigger problem, so have a mechanic take a look.

steps.title: Add oil if it's low
steps.body: Find the oil fill cap on top of the engine. It's a round cap, usually marked with the same oil-can symbol or the words "engine oil." Twist it off, put a funnel in the opening, and pour in about half a quart. Don't pour in the whole bottle at once. Overfilling can actually cause its own problems, so it's better to add a little at a time.

steps.title: Wait, recheck, and close everything up
steps.body: Give the oil a minute to run down into the pan, then check the dipstick again the same way as before. Keep adding a little at a time until the level is near the upper mark. When you're done, push the dipstick back in all the way and screw the fill cap on firmly. A loose cap can let oil splash out while you drive.

wrap_up: If you find yourself adding oil every few weeks, your car is either leaking or burning oil. That's worth mentioning to a mechanic, because it usually gets worse over time and is much cheaper to fix early. Also keep an eye out for dark spots on the ground where you park, which is the most common sign of a leak.

title: Check and fill tire pressure
summary: The right tire pressure improves gas mileage, handling, and tire life. Check it monthly and before long trips.
video_query: how to check and fill tire pressure
intro:
Tires slowly lose air over time, even when nothing is wrong with them, and they lose it faster when the weather turns cold. Driving on tires without enough air makes the car use more gas, wears the tires out faster, makes the steering feel sluggish, and in the worst case can cause a tire to overheat and fail on the highway.

Checking the pressure is quick and costs almost nothing. Plan on doing it once a month and before any long drive.
prep: You'll need a tire pressure gauge, a small tool that tells you how much air is in the tire. A basic pencil-style or digital gauge costs a few dollars at any auto parts store, and it's worth keeping one in your glove box. To add air, most gas stations have an air pump near the edge of the lot. Some are free and some cost a dollar or two in quarters or by card. Many of them have a gauge built into the hose, but your own gauge is usually more accurate.

steps.title: Find the right pressure for your car
steps.body: Open the driver's door and look at the edge of the door frame, where the door latches. You'll find a sticker there that lists the recommended tire pressure, measured in PSI (pounds per square inch). Most cars want somewhere between 30 and 36 PSI. Sometimes the front and rear tires have different numbers. Don't use the number printed on the side of the tire itself; that's the maximum the tire can safely hold, not what your car should run.

steps.title: Check while the tires are cold
steps.body: Driving heats up the air inside the tires, which makes the pressure read a few PSI higher than it really is. For an accurate reading, check first thing in the morning or after the car has been parked for a few hours. If you have to drive to the gas station to add air, that's fine; just know the reading will be a little high, so aim for one or two PSI above the sticker number.

steps.title: Take the cap off the valve stem
steps.body: On each wheel there's a small rubber or metal stem sticking out, about an inch long, with a little cap on the end. This is the valve stem, and it's where air goes in and out. Unscrew the cap and put it somewhere safe, like your pocket, because they're easy to lose.

steps.title: Measure the pressure
steps.body: Press the end of the gauge straight onto the valve stem, firmly and quickly. You'll hear a short hiss of air; if the hissing keeps going, the gauge isn't sealed, so push a little harder or straighten it out. The gauge will show a number. Compare it to the number on the door sticker.

steps.title: Add air if it's low
steps.body: Press the air pump's hose onto the valve stem the same way you did the gauge, and let air flow in for a few seconds at a time. After each short burst, check again with your gauge. It's easy to overshoot, so going slowly saves you time in the end.

steps.title: Let some out if it's too high
steps.body: If you added too much, look at the very center of the valve stem. There's a tiny metal pin there. Press it gently with a fingernail or the back of your gauge, and air will hiss out. Let out a little at a time and recheck until it matches the sticker.

steps.title: Put the cap back on and repeat
steps.body: Screw the valve cap back on so dirt and moisture stay out, then do the same thing for the other three tires. If your car has a spare tire in the trunk, check it every few months too. A flat spare doesn't help much when you need it.

wrap_up: If your car's tire pressure warning light (it looks like a horseshoe with an exclamation point inside) was on, it may take a few minutes of driving after you fill the tires for it to turn off. If one tire keeps losing air week after week, it probably has a slow leak, often from a nail or screw. Tire shops can usually patch that quickly and cheaply, and some do it for free.

title: Check tire tread depth
summary: Worn tread makes it much harder to stop and steer on wet or snowy roads. A coin is all you need to check it.
video_query: how to check tire tread depth penny test
intro:
The grooves cut into your tires, called the tread, are what grip the road. When it rains or snows, those grooves push water out from under the tire so the rubber can stay in contact with the pavement. As tires wear down, the grooves get shallower, and the car takes longer to stop and is much more likely to slide or hydroplane on a wet road.

Tires wear slowly, so it's easy to not notice until it's a problem. A quick check every few months, and before winter, tells you when it's time to start shopping for new ones.
prep: All you need is a penny and a quarter. If you want a more exact measurement, a tread depth gauge costs a few dollars at an auto parts store, but the coins work well for most people.

steps.title: Turn the steering wheel to see the front tires
steps.body: The front tires are tucked into the wheel wells, which makes the tread hard to see. With the car parked, turn the steering wheel all the way to one side. The front of each tire will swing out so you can look at the tread easily. The back tires you can check as they are.

steps.title: Do the penny test
steps.body: Hold a penny so Abraham Lincoln's head is upside down and facing you. Push it, head first, into one of the deepest grooves in the tire. If the tread covers part of Lincoln's head, you have more than 2/32 of an inch of tread left. If you can see the entire top of his head, the tread is worn down to 2/32 of an inch or less. That's the legal limit in most states, and those tires should be replaced right away.

steps.title: Try the quarter test for a stricter check
steps.body: Do the same thing with a quarter, with George Washington's head pointing down into the groove. If the top of his head is visible, your tread is less than 4/32 of an inch. The tires are still legal, but they've lost a lot of their grip in rain and snow, so it's smart to plan on replacing them soon, especially if winter is coming.

steps.title: Check several spots on each tire
steps.body: Tires don't always wear evenly, so test in a few places: near the inside edge, in the middle, and near the outside edge, and at a couple of different spots around the tire. Go by the lowest reading you find.

steps.title: Look for the wear bars
steps.body: If you look closely at the bottom of the grooves, you'll see small raised bars of rubber running across them at intervals. These are called wear bars. When the surface of the tread wears down until it's even with those bars, the tire is worn out. It's a built-in version of the penny test.

steps.title: Notice how the tire is wearing
steps.body: Healthy tires wear down evenly across their whole width. If one edge is much more worn than the other, the car's wheels are probably out of alignment, which means they aren't pointed perfectly straight. If both edges are worn but the middle looks fine, the tire has been running low on air; if only the middle is worn, it's had too much air. Mention any uneven wear to a tire shop when you buy new tires, so the new ones don't wear out the same way.

wrap_up: Also look over the sides of each tire while you're down there. Cracks, bulges, or bubbles in the sidewall mean the tire is damaged inside and could fail, even if the tread looks fine. Have any tire with a bulge looked at right away.

title: Replace wiper blades
summary: Streaking, skipping, or squeaking wipers are worn out. New blades usually snap on in a few minutes with no tools.
video_query: how to replace windshield wiper blades
intro:
Wiper blades are strips of rubber, and sun, heat, and cold slowly harden and crack them. Old blades leave streaks, skip across the glass, squeak, or leave a blurry film that makes it hard to see at night or in the rain. Most blades last about six months to a year.

This is one of the easiest jobs on any car. Auto parts stores will often even do it for you in the parking lot if you buy the blades there, but it's simple enough to do yourself.
prep: You'll need two new wiper blades, and they need to be the right length for your car. The driver's side blade and the passenger's side blade are often different sizes. The easiest way to find the right ones is to ask at an auto parts store or use the lookup on their website: you enter your car's year, make, and model, and it tells you both sizes. Blades range from about $10 to $30 each. Grab a towel too.
safety: When the blade is off, the bare metal wiper arm is spring-loaded. If it slips and snaps down onto the glass, it can crack your windshield. Lay a folded towel on the windshield under the arm while you work, just in case.

steps.title: Lift the wiper arm
steps.body: Pull the first wiper arm up and away from the windshield. It should stay up on its own, standing out from the glass. Lay a folded towel on the windshield underneath it to protect the glass.

steps.title: Find how the blade attaches
steps.body: Look at the middle of the blade, where it connects to the arm. On most cars, the end of the arm is bent into a U-shaped hook, and the blade has a plastic clip that sits inside that hook. There's usually a small tab on the clip that you press to release it.

steps.title: Remove the old blade
steps.body: Press the release tab and slide the blade down, toward the base of the arm, so the clip comes out of the hook. Then tilt the blade and pull it free. It can take a little wiggling the first time. If it won't budge, check the new blade's package; there's usually a diagram showing exactly how your type comes off.

steps.title: Get the new blade ready
steps.body: Open the new blade's packaging. Some blades come with a few different plastic adapters so they can fit many cars. If yours does, compare them to the connector on your wiper arm and use the one that matches. Many blades come with the most common adapter already attached.

steps.title: Attach the new blade
steps.body: Slide the new blade's clip into the hook on the arm, then pull it up into the hook until you hear or feel a click. Give the blade a gentle tug to make sure it's locked in and won't slide off.

steps.title: Lower the arm gently
steps.body: Take the towel out and lower the wiper arm slowly back onto the glass. Don't let it snap down. Then repeat the same steps for the blade on the other side, and the rear wiper if your car has one.

steps.title: Test them
steps.body: Sit in the car, spray some washer fluid, and run the wipers. They should glide smoothly and wipe the glass clean in one pass without streaks or chattering. If one side looks off, double-check that the blade clicked in all the way.

wrap_up: To help new blades last longer, wipe the rubber edge with a damp paper towel every so often, and in winter, don't use the wipers to scrape off ice. Clear the glass with an ice scraper and the defroster first.

title: Refill windshield washer fluid
summary: One of the easiest jobs on a car. Keep the washer fluid full so you can clear road grime and salt in bad weather.
video_query: how to refill windshield washer fluid
intro:
Washer fluid is the cleaning liquid that sprays onto your windshield when you pull the wiper lever. You'll use a lot of it in winter, when road salt and slush coat the glass, and in summer, when bugs pile up. Running out at the wrong moment can leave you squinting through a smeared windshield on the highway.

Refilling it is about as easy as car maintenance gets, so it's a great first job if you've never opened your hood before.
prep: Pick up a jug of windshield washer fluid from any gas station, grocery store, or auto parts store. It usually costs a few dollars. If you live somewhere it freezes in winter, buy a winter or de-icer blend that's rated well below freezing (the label will say something like "-20°F"). A funnel helps but isn't required; most jugs pour cleanly.
safety: Washer fluid is poisonous if swallowed and often brightly colored, so store the jug where kids and pets can't get to it.

steps.title: Open the hood
steps.body: With the car turned off, pull the hood release inside the car, then reach under the front edge of the hood for the second latch and lift the hood up. Use the prop rod to hold it open if your car has one.

steps.title: Find the washer fluid reservoir
steps.body: Look for a plastic cap with a symbol of a windshield with a spray of water coming up onto it. The cap is often blue or white, and it's usually near the front corner of the engine bay. Be careful to pick the right cap; the other caps under the hood are for oil, coolant, and brake fluid, and none of those should ever get washer fluid in them.

steps.title: Fill it up
steps.body: Pop open the cap and pour the washer fluid in until it's close to the top of the opening, or up to the "full" line if the tank has one. The tank holds more than you might expect, sometimes most of a gallon, so don't worry if it takes a while.

steps.title: Close the cap and test the sprayers
steps.body: Snap the cap closed, shut the hood, and try the washer from the driver's seat. If fluid sprays onto the glass, you're done. If nothing comes out, the small nozzles at the base of the windshield might be clogged; a pin or needle can gently clear them.

wrap_up: Avoid filling the tank with plain water, especially in cold climates. Water can freeze in the tank and lines and crack them, and it doesn't clean nearly as well. If you used summer fluid and a cold snap is coming, top off with a winter blend to protect the system.

title: Check your coolant level
summary: Coolant keeps the engine from overheating in summer and freezing in winter. Check the level a few times a year.
video_query: how to check engine coolant level
tools: The right coolant for your car
intro:
An engine produces a huge amount of heat. Coolant, sometimes called antifreeze, is a liquid that flows through the engine, soaks up that heat, and carries it to the radiator at the front of the car, where it cools off. Without enough coolant, the engine can overheat, and an overheated engine can be damaged badly enough that it's not worth repairing.

The system is sealed, so the level shouldn't drop much. Checking it a few times a year, and before summer and winter, catches small leaks before they turn into big problems.
prep: You'll only need coolant if the level turns out to be low. Coolant comes in different types and colors, and they shouldn't be mixed, so check your owner's manual for the exact kind your car uses. The easiest option is a "pre-mixed" or "50/50" jug, which is already diluted with the right amount of water and ready to pour. A rag is helpful too.
safety: Only check coolant when the engine is completely cold. When the engine is warm, the coolant is hot and under pressure, and opening the cap can make it spray out and cause serious burns. The safest time is first thing in the morning, before you've driven anywhere.
Coolant tastes sweet but is poisonous to people and pets. Wipe up any spills right away.

steps.title: Make sure the engine is cold
steps.body: Check before you drive for the day, or after the car has been parked for several hours. If you touch the hood near the engine and it feels warm, wait longer.

steps.title: Find the coolant reservoir
steps.body: Open the hood and look for a see-through plastic tank, usually off to one side near the radiator at the front of the car. It often has a cap with a warning symbol and the words "engine coolant" or a picture of a thermometer. On the side of the tank, you'll see two lines labeled MIN and MAX, or LOW and FULL.

steps.title: Look at the level
steps.body: You don't need to open anything to check. Just look through the side of the plastic tank. The colored liquid inside (it might be green, orange, pink, or blue) should sit somewhere between the two lines. If it does, you're all set.

steps.title: Top it off if it's low
steps.body: If the level is below the MIN line, put a rag over the reservoir cap and turn it slowly. Pour in the coolant your manual recommends until the level reaches the MAX line, then screw the cap back on tightly. Add coolant to this see-through tank, not to the metal radiator cap, unless your manual says otherwise.

steps.title: Watch for signs of a leak
steps.body: If you had to add coolant, check again in a week or two. A level that keeps dropping, colorful puddles under the front of the car, a sweet syrupy smell after driving, or a temperature gauge that climbs higher than usual are all signs of a leak. Get those looked at by a mechanic soon.

wrap_up: If your temperature gauge ever moves into the red, or you see steam coming from under the hood, pull over somewhere safe and turn the engine off. Don't open the hood or the coolant cap until it has cooled down, and call for help rather than continuing to drive.

title: Replace the engine air filter
summary: A clogged air filter can hurt acceleration and fuel economy. Swapping it is usually a few clips and no tools.
video_query: how to replace engine air filter
intro:
Your engine breathes in a lot of air to burn fuel, and the engine air filter keeps dust, dirt, leaves, and bugs from getting sucked inside along with it. Over time the filter fills up, and a clogged filter can make the engine work harder, which can hurt acceleration and gas mileage.

Most cars need a new air filter about once a year or every 15,000 to 30,000 miles, more often if you drive on dirt roads. Shops often charge $40 or more to swap it, but the part is usually under $25 and the job takes minutes.
prep: Buy an engine air filter that fits your car; an auto parts store can look it up by year, make, and model. Most filter boxes close with metal clips, so you won't need tools, but some use a few screws, so having a screwdriver nearby doesn't hurt. A rag or a shop vacuum is handy for cleaning out the box.

steps.title: Find the air filter box
steps.body: With the engine off, open the hood. Look for a large black plastic box, often near the front or side of the engine bay, with a big, wide tube running from it toward the engine. That box is the air filter housing.

steps.title: Open the box
steps.body: The lid is held down by metal spring clips or a few screws around the edges. Flip the clips open with your fingers, or remove the screws, and lift the lid up. Sometimes the lid stays attached to the tube, so you may only be able to lift it partway. That's fine.

steps.title: Take out the old filter
steps.body: Lift the filter straight out. Before you set it aside, notice which way it was sitting, because the new one goes in the same way. The filter is usually a flat rectangle of pleated paper surrounded by a rubber rim.

steps.title: Decide if it really needs replacing
steps.body: Hold the old filter up toward a light. A clean filter is white or light gray, and you can see light through it. If it's dark gray or brown, packed with dirt, or full of leaves and bugs, it's done. If you bought a new one anyway, go ahead and replace it.

steps.title: Clean out the box
steps.body: Wipe out any loose dirt, leaves, or debris from the bottom of the box with a rag or a vacuum. Be careful not to knock anything into the opening that leads toward the engine; anything that falls in there goes straight to the engine.

steps.title: Drop in the new filter
steps.body: Set the new filter in the box facing the same way the old one was. Press around the rubber edge so it sits flat and snug all the way around. If there are gaps, dirty air can slip around the filter, which defeats the purpose.

steps.title: Close it up
steps.body: Lower the lid back into place and fasten every clip or screw. Run your finger around the edge to make sure the lid is fully seated with no gaps. That's it.

wrap_up: Write down the date and your mileage so you know when you last changed it. While you're at the parts store, consider grabbing a cabin air filter too; it's a different filter, and it's just as easy to replace.

title: Replace the cabin air filter
summary: This filter cleans the air coming through your vents. A dirty one causes weak airflow and musty smells.
video_query: how to replace cabin air filter
intro:
The cabin air filter cleans the air that blows into the car through your vents, catching dust, pollen, and pollution before you breathe it. When it gets clogged, the air coming out of the vents gets weak even with the fan on high, the windows take longer to defog, and the car can start to smell musty.

Most cars should get a new one about once a year. It's usually hidden behind the glove box and takes no tools.
prep: Buy a cabin air filter that fits your car (an auto parts store can look it up for you). They usually cost $15 to $30. A flashlight helps you see behind the glove box. It's also worth a quick look at your owner's manual, since it will show exactly where your car's filter is.

steps.title: Find where your filter lives
steps.body: In most cars, the cabin filter sits behind the glove box. In some, it's under the hood, beneath a plastic panel at the base of the windshield. Your owner's manual will say which; search it for "cabin air filter" or "climate control filter." The steps below are for the more common behind-the-glove-box location.

steps.title: Empty the glove box and let it drop down
steps.body: Take everything out of the glove box and open it. On the sides, there are small stops that keep it from falling open too far. Gently squeeze the sides of the glove box inward, or pop out the little pins or tabs, so it can swing down past them. If there's a thin arm on one side (a damper that slows the door), unhook it. The glove box will now hang down, out of the way.

steps.title: Open the filter cover
steps.body: Behind where the glove box was, you'll see a narrow rectangular plastic cover, a few inches tall and about a foot wide. Squeeze the clips on its sides or press the tabs, and pull it off.

steps.title: Slide out the old filter
steps.body: Pull the old filter straight out. Before you toss it, look at its edge for a printed arrow labeled "air flow" or "up." Notice which direction it points, because the new filter needs to face the same way. Don't be surprised if the old one is gray and full of leaves.

steps.title: Slide in the new filter
steps.body: Check the arrow on the new filter and point it the same way the old one pointed. Slide it in gently and evenly. It should go all the way in without bending.

steps.title: Put everything back
steps.body: Snap the cover back on, lift the glove box back into place so the stops catch again, and reattach the damper arm if there was one. Then turn the fan on high. You should feel noticeably stronger airflow if the old filter was dirty.

wrap_up: If your car still smells musty after a new filter, the smell may be coming from moisture in the air conditioning system. An A/C cleaning spray, or a shop, can help with that.

title: Replace a headlight or taillight bulb
summary: A burned-out bulb can get you pulled over. On many cars it's a twist-and-pull job from under the hood or through the trunk.
intro:
Working lights help you see at night and help other drivers see you, and a burned-out headlight, taillight, or brake light is also an easy reason for police to pull you over. On many cars, replacing a bulb is a quick twist-and-pull job from under the hood or inside the trunk.

On some newer cars, though, the bulbs are packed in tightly or the lights use LEDs that aren't meant to be replaced on their own. If you can't reach the bulb without taking apart the bumper, a shop can usually do it quickly.
prep: Every light on a car uses a specific bulb with its own part number, like H11 or 7443. Find yours in the owner's manual (look for a "bulb specifications" table), or have an auto parts store look it up by your car's year, make, and model. A pair of clean gloves or a paper towel will keep your fingers off the new bulb. On some cars, you'll also need a screwdriver to remove a cover.
safety: Turn the car and the lights off before you start. Bulbs get very hot, so if the light was just on, give it a few minutes to cool.

steps.title: Find the back of the light
steps.body: For a headlight, open the hood and look behind the headlight, at the side of it facing the engine. For a taillight, open the trunk; there's usually a small fabric or plastic panel on the side you can pull back, or a few screws holding the light in place. You're looking for the back of the light housing, where a round cap or a plastic socket with a wire attached sticks out.

steps.title: Unplug the wire connector
steps.body: The bulb has a plastic plug attached to it with wires. Press the small tab on the plug and pull it straight off the bulb. It might be snug, so wiggle it gently rather than yanking on the wires.

steps.title: Remove the old bulb
steps.body: Most bulbs come out by turning them a quarter turn counterclockwise (to the left) and pulling them straight out. Some are held by a thin wire spring clip that you press and swing aside first. If there's a round rubber or plastic cap covering the back, twist that off first.

steps.title: Handle the new bulb carefully
steps.body: Hold the new bulb by its plastic or metal base, not the glass. This matters most for headlight bulbs, which are usually halogen. The natural oils on your skin create hot spots on the glass that can make the bulb crack or burn out early. If you accidentally touch it, wipe the glass with a little rubbing alcohol.

steps.title: Put in the new bulb and reconnect it
steps.body: Slide the new bulb into the opening, then turn it clockwise (to the right) until it locks, or secure the spring clip. Push the wire connector back on until it clicks, and replace any cap or cover you removed.

steps.title: Test it
steps.body: Turn on the lights and walk around the car to check that the new bulb works. For brake lights, have a friend press the brake pedal while you look, or back up close to a garage door or window and look for the red glow in your mirror.

wrap_up: Headlight bulbs get dimmer as they age, so when one burns out, the other is usually close behind. Replacing both at the same time keeps your lights even and saves you from doing the job twice.

title: Change your oil and filter
summary: The single most important maintenance job. Doing it yourself saves money and teaches you a lot about your car.
video_query: how to change oil and oil filter
tools: Wrench or socket for the drain plug
Ramps or a floor jack and jack stands
intro:
Engine oil breaks down as you drive. It gets dirty, thins out, and stops protecting the engine as well as it should. Changing it on schedule is the single most important thing you can do to keep an engine running for a long time. Most modern cars need an oil change every 5,000 to 10,000 miles, and your owner's manual or the car's maintenance reminder will tell you the right interval.

The job involves getting under the car, so it takes more setup than the other easy guides. But once you've done it once or twice, it becomes routine, and you'll save money every time.
prep:
Start with your owner's manual. Look up the type of oil (like 0W-20 or 5W-30) and how much your engine holds, called its capacity (for example, 4.4 quarts). At an auto parts store, buy that much of that oil, plus an oil filter made for your car and a new drain plug washer. The washer is a small metal or rubber ring, sometimes called a crush washer, that seals the drain plug; the store can find the right one.

You'll also need a wrench or socket that fits your drain plug (often 14 mm or 17 mm), an oil filter wrench (a tool that grips the round filter), a drain pan that holds at least 6 quarts, a funnel, gloves, and rags. To get under the car safely, use a pair of drive-up car ramps, or a floor jack plus two jack stands. Wheel chocks, small wedges that keep the wheels from rolling, are cheap and worth having.
safety: Never get under a car that's held up only by a jack. Jacks can slip or fail without warning. Always use ramps or jack stands, and always on solid, flat ground like a driveway or garage floor, never on grass or gravel.
Oil that was just in a running engine can be hot enough to burn. If you've been driving, let the car sit for 20 to 30 minutes first. Warm oil drains better, but hot oil can hurt you.
Used oil is toxic and can't be thrown in the trash or poured down a drain. Most auto parts stores take used oil and old filters for free.

steps.title: Get the car ready
steps.body: Park on a flat, solid surface and set the parking brake. If the engine is cold, start it and let it run for two or three minutes; slightly warm oil flows out faster and carries more dirt with it. Then turn it off. Put wheel chocks behind the back tires so the car can't roll.

steps.title: Raise the front of the car safely
steps.body: If you have ramps, line them up in front of the front tires and drive up onto them slowly until the tires settle into the dip at the top. If you're using a jack, lift the car at the jack points shown in your owner's manual, then set it down onto jack stands placed under the car's frame. Push on the car firmly before going underneath to make sure it's stable.

steps.title: Loosen the oil fill cap
steps.body: Open the hood and twist off the oil fill cap on top of the engine (it's marked with an oil-can symbol). Leaving it off lets air in from the top, so the old oil drains out faster and more smoothly, the same way a can of juice pours better with two holes.

steps.title: Find the drain plug
steps.body: Slide under the front of the car with a flashlight. The oil pan is a metal pan at the very bottom of the engine, and the drain plug is a single bolt on its lowest point. Be careful not to confuse it with the transmission's drain plug, which is usually farther back on a separate pan. If you're not sure which is which, your owner's manual or a video for your exact car will show it.

steps.title: Drain the old oil
steps.body: Slide the drain pan underneath the plug, a little toward the front, because the oil will come out at an angle. Turn the plug counterclockwise with your wrench to loosen it, then unscrew it the rest of the way by hand. As the last threads come free, pull the plug away quickly so the oil doesn't run down your arm. Let it drain until it slows to an occasional drip, about 5 to 10 minutes.

steps.title: Put the drain plug back in
steps.body: Wipe the plug clean, slide the new washer onto it, and thread it back in by hand. Hand-threading first makes sure it doesn't go in crooked. Then tighten it with the wrench until it's snug, plus a little more. Don't crank on it as hard as you can. The oil pan is often soft metal, and stripping its threads turns a $40 job into a several-hundred-dollar repair.

steps.title: Remove the old oil filter
steps.body: The oil filter is a round canister about the size of a soup can, screwed onto the side or bottom of the engine. Move the drain pan underneath it. Fit the filter wrench around it, turn it counterclockwise to break it loose, then spin it off by hand. It will be full of oil, so tip it open-side-up into the pan as soon as it comes off.

steps.title: Check for the old gasket
steps.body: Look at the spot on the engine where the filter was. Every filter has a round rubber ring, called a gasket, that seals against the engine. Make sure the old gasket came off with the old filter. If it stuck to the engine, peel it off. Leaving it there and adding a new filter on top creates a double gasket that will leak badly. Wipe the area clean.

steps.title: Install the new filter
steps.body: Dip a finger in some of your new oil and wipe a thin layer onto the new filter's rubber gasket. This helps it seal and makes it easier to remove next time. Screw the new filter on by hand until the gasket touches the engine, then turn it about three-quarters of a turn more, still by hand. Filters only need to be hand-tight; using the wrench to tighten it can make it nearly impossible to remove later.

steps.title: Lower the car and add new oil
steps.body: Gather your tools, pull the drain pan out, and carefully lower the car back to flat ground. Put a funnel in the oil fill opening and pour in new oil, stopping about half a quart short of your engine's full capacity. You'll top off the rest after checking the level.

steps.title: Check the level
steps.body: Wait a minute for the oil to settle, then check the dipstick the same way you would for a regular oil check: pull it, wipe it, push it back in, and pull it again. Add a little oil at a time until the level is near the upper mark. Then put the fill cap back on firmly.

steps.title: Run the engine and look for leaks
steps.body: Start the engine and let it run for about 30 seconds. The oil pressure light on your dashboard should go off within a few seconds. While it's running, look under the car at the drain plug and the filter for any drips. If you see a drip, turn the engine off and snug the leaking part slightly more.

steps.title: Final check and clean up
steps.body: Turn the engine off, wait a few minutes, and check the dipstick one last time, adding a little if needed. Pour the used oil from the drain pan into the empty oil bottles, and take them and the old filter to an auto parts store for recycling. Finally, reset your car's oil life or maintenance reminder (your owner's manual explains how), and write down the date and mileage.

wrap_up: Your first oil change will probably take over an hour, and that's completely normal. By the third one, most people can do it in about half an hour. If anything about getting under the car makes you uneasy, a quick-lube shop is a perfectly good option, and you can still use this guide to understand what they're doing.

title: Rotate your tires
summary: Moving tires to different positions helps them wear evenly and last longer. Most cars need it every 5,000 to 7,500 miles.
intro:
Your front tires and back tires don't wear at the same speed. On most cars, the front tires do most of the steering and braking, so they wear faster. Rotating the tires means moving them to different spots on the car so they all wear down evenly, which helps the whole set last longer and keeps the car handling predictably.

Most cars need a rotation every 5,000 to 7,500 miles, which lines up nicely with every oil change. Many tire shops do it for free if you bought your tires there, so it's worth asking before you do it yourself.
prep:
You'll need a floor jack to lift the car and jack stands to hold it up safely while the wheels are off. With two stands you can do one side of the car at a time, and four make it easier. You'll also need a lug wrench or a breaker bar (a long-handled wrench) with a socket that fits your lug nuts, the nuts that hold each wheel on. A torque wrench lets you tighten the lug nuts to the exact amount your car calls for; you can borrow one free from many auto parts stores. Wheel chocks and a tire pressure gauge round out the list.

Check your owner's manual for two things: the rotation pattern your car uses, and the lug nut torque, a number in foot-pounds like 80 ft-lbs.
safety: Never put any part of your body under a car that's held up only by a jack. Lower it onto jack stands before you take a wheel off.
Work on flat, solid ground, like a driveway or garage floor. A jack can sink into grass or slide on gravel or a slope.

steps.title: Learn your rotation pattern
steps.body: Your owner's manual shows which tire moves where. On most front-wheel-drive cars, the front tires move straight back to the rear, and the rear tires cross over to the opposite sides of the front (rear left goes to front right, and rear right goes to front left). Rear-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive cars often use a different pattern. If your tires have an arrow on the sidewall, they're directional and must stay on the same side of the car, so they only swap front to back.

steps.title: Park and chock the wheels
steps.body: Park on flat ground and set the parking brake. Put wheel chocks against the tires on the opposite end from where you'll lift first, so the car can't roll.

steps.title: Loosen the lug nuts while the car is on the ground
steps.body: Before lifting anything, use your lug wrench to loosen each lug nut on the wheels you're about to move, about half a turn counterclockwise. Don't take them off yet. Doing this while the tire is on the ground keeps the wheel from spinning while you push on the wrench. If your wheels have plastic hubcaps, pry those off first.

steps.title: Lift the car and set it on jack stands
steps.body: Place the floor jack under the lift point shown in your owner's manual. These are reinforced spots on the car's frame, often marked by small notches near each wheel. Jack the car up until the tires are a couple of inches off the ground, slide a jack stand under the frame near the jack, and slowly lower the car onto the stand. Give the car a firm push to make sure it's steady.

steps.title: Move the wheels
steps.body: Unscrew the lug nuts the rest of the way and pull each wheel off. Wheels are heavier than they look, so lift with your legs. Move each wheel to its new position following your rotation pattern.

steps.title: Start the lug nuts by hand
steps.body: Line up the holes in the wheel with the bolts, push the wheel on, and thread each lug nut on by hand first so none of them go on crooked. Then snug them with the wrench in a star pattern: tighten one, then the one across from it, and so on, rather than going around in a circle. This pulls the wheel on evenly.

steps.title: Lower the car and tighten fully
steps.body: Raise the car slightly off the jack stand, remove the stand, and lower the car to the ground. Now use the torque wrench, set to the number from your owner's manual, and tighten each lug nut in the same star pattern until the wrench clicks. Lug nuts that are too loose can let a wheel come off, and nuts that are too tight can warp the brakes.

steps.title: Set the tire pressure
steps.body: After rotating, check all four tires with your gauge and adjust them to the pressures listed on the driver's door sticker. Some cars use different pressures for the front and back, and the tires just swapped places.

steps.title: Recheck after a short drive
steps.body: After driving about 50 miles, go back over the lug nuts with the torque wrench one more time. Wheels can settle slightly once they're driven on, and this quick double-check makes sure everything stays tight.

wrap_up: A rotation is also the perfect time to look over each tire up close for nails, cracks, bulges, or uneven wear, and to peek at your brake pads through the open wheel well.

title: Clean and test your battery
summary: Corroded terminals and a weak battery are the most common causes of a car that won't start. Check it before winter.
video_query: how to clean car battery terminals and test battery
intro:
Your car's battery provides the burst of power that starts the engine. Over time, a crusty buildup called corrosion can form on the battery's metal connection points, called terminals, and that buildup gets in the way of the electricity. Batteries also simply wear out, usually after 3 to 5 years. Both are among the most common reasons a car won't start, and cold weather makes them worse.

Cleaning the terminals and testing the battery before winter can save you from being stuck in a parking lot on the coldest morning of the year.
prep: Battery acid can burn skin and eyes, so start with safety glasses and a pair of gloves. You'll need a wrench that fits the bolts on the battery's cable clamps (10 mm is very common), a wire brush or a battery terminal brush (a few dollars at a parts store), baking soda, and a cup of water. A multimeter, an inexpensive tool that measures electricity, lets you test the battery yourself, but it's optional because many auto parts stores will test it for free.
safety: Wear your glasses and gloves the whole time, and avoid touching your face while you work.
Batteries can give off a flammable gas, so keep sparks, cigarettes, and flames away.

Never let a metal tool touch both battery terminals at the same time, or touch the positive terminal and any metal part of the car at the same time. That creates a short circuit that can spark, damage the battery, or burn you.

steps.title: Turn the car off and find the battery
steps.body: Turn the car completely off and take the key out. Open the hood and find the battery, a rectangular box usually in a front corner of the engine bay. On some cars it's under a plastic cover, and on a few it's in the trunk or under a seat; your owner's manual will say.

steps.title: Look it over
steps.body: The battery has two terminals on top: positive, marked with a plus sign (+) and usually a red cover or cable, and negative, marked with a minus sign (-) and usually a black cable. Look for white, green, or bluish crusty buildup around them. That's corrosion. Also check the battery case itself. If it's cracked, leaking, or the sides are swollen or bulging, stop here and have the battery replaced.

steps.title: Disconnect the negative cable first
steps.body: Use your wrench to loosen the nut on the negative (-) clamp, then twist and lift the clamp off the terminal. Always disconnect the negative side first. If your wrench happens to touch the car's metal body while you work on the positive side later, nothing will spark. Tuck the cable aside so it can't flop back onto the terminal.

steps.title: Then disconnect the positive cable
steps.body: Do the same for the positive (+) clamp: loosen the nut, lift the clamp off, and move it out of the way.

steps.title: Scrub away the corrosion
steps.body: Stir about a tablespoon of baking soda into a cup of water. Dip your brush in it and scrub the battery terminals and the inside of each cable clamp. The mixture will fizz as it neutralizes the acid, which is exactly what you want. Keep scrubbing until the metal is shiny.

steps.title: Rinse and dry
steps.body: Wipe away the gunk with a rag dampened in plain water, then dry everything with a clean rag. Try not to let a lot of water run down into the engine bay.

steps.title: Reconnect positive first, then negative
steps.body: Put the cables back in the opposite order: the positive (+) clamp first, then the negative (-) clamp. Push each clamp all the way down onto its terminal and tighten the nut until you can't twist the clamp by hand. A loose clamp can cause the same starting problems as corrosion.

steps.title: Test the battery
steps.body: If you have a multimeter, set it to measure DC volts (the setting marked V with a straight line). With the engine off, touch the red probe to the positive terminal and the black probe to the negative terminal. A fully charged battery reads about 12.6 volts. Around 12.4 is fine. Below about 12.2 means the battery is weak and should be charged and tested further.

steps.title: Get a professional test if you're unsure
steps.body: A multimeter only shows how charged the battery is, not how well it holds up under the heavy load of starting the engine. Most auto parts stores will do that deeper test for free, often right in the parking lot. If your battery is more than 4 or 5 years old, it's worth getting tested before winter.

wrap_up: Disconnecting the battery may reset your radio stations and clock, and on some cars the engine may idle a little unevenly for the first few minutes while its computer relearns. That's normal. A thin layer of petroleum jelly or a terminal protector spray on the clean terminals helps keep corrosion from coming back.

title: Jump-start a dead battery
summary: Know this before you need it. With jumper cables and a second car, you can get going in a few minutes.
video_query: how to jump start a car
tools: Jumper cables or a portable jump starter
intro:
If you turn the key and hear clicking, or the dashboard lights up but the engine won't turn over, the battery has probably run down. It happens to everyone eventually, often after leaving headlights or an interior light on. A jump-start borrows power from another car's battery for long enough to get your engine running.

It's worth reading this before you ever need it, so you're not figuring it out in a dark parking lot.
prep: You'll need a set of jumper cables and a second car with a working battery. Jumper cables are two thick wires with big metal clamps on each end, one red and one black. A set costs around $20 to $30 and is worth keeping in your trunk. A portable jump starter, a small battery pack with its own clamps, is a great alternative because you don't need a second car; just follow the instructions that come with it.
safety: Don't try to jump a battery that is cracked, leaking, or frozen. Call for roadside help instead.
Once the cables are connected to a car, never let the metal clamps touch each other.
Hybrids and electric cars have their own procedures for jump-starting. Check the owner's manual before jumping one, or before using one to jump another car.

steps.title: Position the cars
steps.body: Park the working car close to the car with the dead battery, either nose to nose or side by side, so the cables can reach both batteries. The cars should be close but not touching. Turn off both cars, set both parking brakes, and open both hoods.

steps.title: Find the battery terminals on both cars
steps.body: On each battery, find the positive terminal, marked with a plus sign (+) and usually a red cover, and the negative terminal, marked with a minus sign (-). If there's a plastic cover over the positive terminal, flip it open.

steps.title: Connect red to the dead battery
steps.body: Take one of the red clamps and attach it to the positive (+) terminal of the dead battery. Squeeze it open and let it bite down firmly onto the metal.

steps.title: Connect red to the good battery
steps.body: Take the other red clamp, on the opposite end of the cables, and attach it to the positive (+) terminal of the working car's battery.

steps.title: Connect black to the good battery
steps.body: Attach one black clamp to the negative (-) terminal of the working car's battery.

steps.title: Connect the last black clamp to bare metal on the dead car
steps.body: This is the step people most often get wrong. Instead of clipping the last black clamp onto the dead battery, attach it to a bare, unpainted metal surface on the dead car's engine or frame, like a thick bolt or bracket, a foot or more away from the battery. This is called grounding. It completes the circuit just the same, but any small spark happens away from the battery, which is safer.

steps.title: Start the working car
steps.body: Start the car with the good battery and let it run for two or three minutes. This sends some charge into the dead battery.

steps.title: Try to start the dead car
steps.body: Now try starting the car with the dead battery. If it starts, great. If it only clicks, let the working car run a few more minutes, check that all four clamps are tight, and try again. If it still won't start after a few tries, the problem may be something other than the battery.

steps.title: Remove the cables in reverse order
steps.body: With both cars running, take the cables off in the opposite order you put them on: the black clamp from the bare metal first, then the black clamp from the good battery, then the red clamp from the good battery, and last the red clamp from the battery that was dead. Keep the clamps from touching each other or any metal as you remove them.

steps.title: Keep the car running
steps.body: Drive the car that was jumped for at least 20 to 30 minutes, ideally on the highway, so its charging system can refill the battery. If you turn it off right away, it may not start again.

wrap_up: A battery that needed a jump once because a light was left on is usually fine. But if it dies again, or the car was hard to start for a while beforehand, have the battery and charging system tested. Many auto parts stores do it for free.

title: Check your brake pads
summary: Learn the signs of worn brakes and how to see how much pad is left, so you can replace them before they damage the rotors.
tools: Floor jack, jack stands, and lug wrench, optional
intro:
When you press the brake pedal, brake pads squeeze against a metal disc attached to each wheel, called a rotor, and the friction slows the car down. The pads are designed to wear away slowly, and they need to be replaced every so often, typically somewhere between 25,000 and 70,000 miles depending on the car and how you drive. If they wear all the way down, metal grinds on metal, which damages the rotors, turns a modest repair into an expensive one, and makes the car take longer to stop.

You don't need to be a mechanic to keep an eye on them. Knowing what to listen for, and how to take a quick look, helps you catch worn pads in time.
prep: For a quick look, all you need is a flashlight. For a clearer view, you'll want to take a wheel off, which needs a floor jack, a jack stand, and a lug wrench, the same tools as a tire rotation. Doing this check during a tire rotation is the easiest time, since the wheels are already off.
safety: If you hear a grinding noise when braking, the brake pedal feels soft or sinks toward the floor, or the brake warning light is on, don't wait. Have the brakes checked right away and drive as little as possible until then.
If you take a wheel off, the car must be resting on a jack stand, never only on a jack.
Actually replacing brake pads is a job for an experienced DIYer or a shop. Brakes are the most important safety system on your car, so there's no shame in leaving that part to a professional.

steps.title: Listen while you drive
steps.body: Many brake pads have a small metal tab built in that starts to squeal against the rotor when the pad gets thin. If you hear a high-pitched squeal when you press the brakes, especially one that stops when you let go, your pads are likely getting low. A deeper grinding or growling sound is more serious; it usually means the pads are completely worn and metal is rubbing on metal.

steps.title: Pay attention to how the car feels
steps.body: Other warning signs include the car pulling to one side when you brake, a vibration or pulsing in the brake pedal or steering wheel, or the car taking noticeably longer to stop than it used to. Any of these is a good reason to have the brakes inspected.

steps.title: Take a look through the wheel
steps.body: Park the car, and turn the steering wheel to one side if you're checking the front brakes so you can see in more easily. Shine a flashlight through the openings in the wheel. You'll see a large, flat, shiny metal disc, which is the rotor, and a bulky clamp wrapped around its edge, which is the caliper. The brake pads sit inside the caliper, pressed against both sides of the rotor.

steps.title: Find the pad and judge its thickness
steps.body: Look at the edge of the caliper where it meets the rotor. You'll see a metal backing plate and, between that plate and the rotor, a layer of darker friction material. That layer is the pad. New pads have about a third of an inch to half an inch of material. If what's left looks thinner than about an eighth of an inch (3 mm), roughly the thickness of two stacked pennies, it's time for new pads.

steps.title: Take the wheel off for a better view, if needed
steps.body: If you can't see the pad clearly through the wheel, loosen the lug nuts, lift that corner of the car with the jack, set it on a jack stand, and remove the wheel. Now you'll have an unobstructed view of the caliper and both edges of the pad.

steps.title: Look at the rotor too
steps.body: While you're looking, check the rotor's surface. A healthy rotor is smooth and evenly shiny. Deep grooves you can feel with a fingernail, a raised lip around the outer edge, or bluish discolored patches from overheating mean the rotors may need to be resurfaced or replaced along with the pads.

steps.title: Check the brake fluid
steps.body: Under the hood, find the brake fluid reservoir, a small see-through plastic container usually near the back of the engine bay on the driver's side, with MIN and MAX lines. The fluid level drops slowly as pads wear, which is normal. A sudden drop, though, can mean a leak, and that needs attention right away.

steps.title: Put everything back
steps.body: If you removed a wheel, put it back on, start the lug nuts by hand, lower the car, and tighten the lug nuts to the torque in your owner's manual using a star pattern.

wrap_up: Brakes are usually checked when you get your tires rotated, so asking the shop to tell you how much pad is left is an easy way to stay ahead of it. When you do replace pads, it's normal for a mechanic to suggest new rotors at the same time if the old ones are worn.

title: Replace spark plugs
summary: Worn spark plugs cause rough idling, misfires, and poor fuel economy. On many 4-cylinder engines this is a doable afternoon job.
intro:
Spark plugs create the small spark that ignites the fuel inside each of your engine's cylinders, thousands of times a minute. Over time, their tips wear down and the spark gets weaker. Worn plugs can cause a rough or shaky idle, hesitation when you accelerate, worse gas mileage, a harder time starting, and eventually a check engine light for a misfire.

Modern spark plugs last a long time, often 60,000 to 100,000 miles. On many 4-cylinder engines the plugs sit right on top and are easy to reach, which makes this a satisfying afternoon project. On some engines, especially many V6s, a few plugs are buried under other parts, and that's a job best left to a shop.
prep:
Look in your owner's manual for three things: the exact spark plug your engine uses, the gap (the tiny space at the tip of the plug, in thousandths of an inch or millimeters), and the tightening torque. Buy one plug per cylinder; a 4-cylinder engine needs four.

Tools-wise, you'll need a ratchet with a few extensions, a spark plug socket (a deep socket with a rubber insert inside that grips the plug so it doesn't fall), and a torque wrench so you tighten the plugs exactly the right amount. A spark plug gap gauge costs a dollar or two. Compressed air or a vacuum helps clean around the plugs before you remove them, and a small tube of dielectric grease is a nice extra.
safety: Only do this on a completely cold engine. Spark plugs screw into soft aluminum on most engines, and taking them out while it's hot can damage the threads, which is an expensive repair. Let the car sit for several hours, or overnight, first.
Before you start, look up a video for your exact engine. If it shows removing the intake manifold or other major parts to reach the plugs, have a shop do it instead.

steps.title: Let the engine cool and take off the cover
steps.body: Make sure the engine is fully cold. Open the hood. Many engines have a plastic cover on top that pops off by pulling up firmly or by removing a couple of bolts. Under it, you'll see a row of ignition coils, one for each cylinder, or on older cars, thick rubber wires leading down into the engine. The spark plugs sit underneath those.

steps.title: Work on one cylinder at a time
steps.body: This is the most important habit for this job. Fully finish one spark plug, from removing the old one to putting the coil back, before moving on to the next. That way you can never mix up which wire or coil goes where.

steps.title: Remove the first ignition coil
steps.body: Find the electrical connector plugged into the top of the first coil. Press its tab and pull it straight off. Then remove the small bolt holding the coil in place, and pull the coil straight up and out. It may be snug, so a gentle twist while pulling helps. On older cars with plug wires, grab the rubber boot at the end of the wire, not the wire itself, and twist and pull.

steps.title: Clean out the spark plug well
steps.body: Now you're looking down a tube into the engine, with the top of the spark plug at the bottom. Before removing the plug, blow out any dirt or debris with compressed air, or vacuum it out. When the plug comes out, there's an open hole straight into the cylinder, and anything that falls in can damage the engine.

steps.title: Remove the old spark plug
steps.body: Put the spark plug socket on your extension and ratchet, slide it down the well, and press until it seats over the plug. Turn it counterclockwise to loosen the plug. It may take a firm push to break it free at first. Once it's loose, unscrew it the rest of the way and lift it out; the rubber insert in the socket holds it.

steps.title: Check the gap on the new plug
steps.body: Look up the correct gap in your owner's manual and check it with the gap gauge by sliding the gauge between the two metal tips at the end of the plug. Many plugs come correctly gapped from the factory. If you have iridium or platinum plugs, don't try to adjust the gap by bending the thin center tip, because it breaks easily. If the gap is off, exchange the plug.

steps.title: Thread the new plug in by hand
steps.body: Put the new plug into the socket and lower it into the well. Using only the extension, without the ratchet attached, turn it clockwise slowly by hand. It should spin in smoothly several full turns before it gets snug. If it feels hard to turn right away, it may be going in crooked, called cross-threading, so back it out and try again. A short piece of rubber hose pushed onto the end of the plug is an old trick that makes this easier.

steps.title: Tighten it to the right torque
steps.body: Attach your torque wrench, set it to the number from your owner's manual, and tighten the plug until the wrench clicks. Don't tighten past that. Too tight can strip the threads in the engine, and too loose can let the plug work its way out.

steps.title: Reinstall the coil
steps.body: If you have dielectric grease, put a small dab inside the rubber end of the coil; it helps keep moisture out and makes the coil easier to remove next time. Push the coil back down onto the plug until it seats, reinstall its bolt, and press the electrical connector back on until it clicks.

steps.title: Repeat for the remaining cylinders
steps.body: Move on to the next cylinder and repeat the same steps, one at a time, until every plug is replaced. Then put the engine cover back on.

steps.title: Start the engine and listen
steps.body: Start the car. It should idle smoothly and evenly. If the engine shakes or runs rough, or the check engine light comes on, the most likely cause is a coil connector that isn't fully clicked in. Turn the engine off and press each connector firmly to make sure.

wrap_up: Look at the old plugs before you throw them out; their tips can tell a mechanic a lot about how the engine is running. Oily, black, or very white tips are worth mentioning at your next service. And write down your mileage, since you probably won't need to do this again for a long time.
